{{Infobox person|gender={{ill|Male (gender)|qid=Q6581097}}|children={{ill|Kamitsukeno no Tamichi|qid=Q11359475}}; {{ill|Utsufuruno-mikoto|qid=Q108679309}}; {{ill|Takehase|qid=Q17209207}}|father={{ill|Mimorowake|qid=Q17230461|2=ja|3=御諸別王|lt=Mimorowake|4=zh|5=御諸別王|qid=Q17230461}}}}

'''Aratawake''' (荒田別, also 大荒田別命) was a figure from Japan's {{ill|Kofun period|en|Kofun period|qid=Q459939|lt=Kofun period}}, recorded in texts such as the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|en|Nihon Shoki|qid=Q813935|lt=Nihon Shoki}}. He is described as an ancestor of the {{ill|Kamitsukeno clan|ja|上毛野氏|1=Kamitsukeno clan|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kamitsukeno clan|13=User:Immanuelle/Kamitsukeno clan|qq=}}, a military commander serving {{ill|Empress Jingū|en|Empress Jingū|qid=Q232803|lt=Empress Jingū}} and {{ill|Emperor Ōjin|en|Emperor Ōjin|qid=Q317997|lt=Emperor Ōjin}} (15th Emperor of Japan).
== Historical Accounts ==
According to the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|en|Nihon Shoki|qid=Q813935|lt=Nihon Shoki}}, in the 49th year of {{ill|Empress Jingū|en|Empress Jingū|qid=Q232803|lt=Empress Jingū}}’s reign (traditional date), Aratawake, along with Kagawawake, was appointed as a general and participated in the conquest of {{ill|Silla|en|Silla|qid=Q28456|lt=Silla}}. It is recorded that they returned to Japan in the second month of her 50th year.
In the 15th year of {{ill|Emperor Ōjin|en|Emperor Ōjin|qid=Q317997|lt=Emperor Ōjin}}’s reign, Aratawake was dispatched to [[:en:Baekje|Baekje]] alongside Hikoitsuse. The following year, they returned to Japan accompanied by the scholar {{ill|Wani (scholar)|en|Wani (scholar)|qid=Q482722|lt=Wani}}. The record explicitly describes Aratawake and Hikoitsuse as "ancestors of the Kamitsukeno clan."
According to the {{ill|Shinsen Shōjiroku|en|Shinsen Shōjiroku|qid=Q1045362|lt=Shinsen Shōjiroku}}, Aratawake is listed as the father of {{ill|Kamitsukeno no Tamichi|ja|上毛野田道|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kamitsukeno no Tamichi|qq=}}. The Nihon Shoki further notes that Tamichi was a younger brother of {{ill|Takehase|ja|竹葉瀬|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Takehase|qq=}}, who is also identified in genealogical records as a son of Aratawake.
The {{ill|Shoku Nihongi|en|Shoku Nihongi|qid=Q611399|lt=Shoku Nihongi}} mentions Aratawake in relation to a petition by {{ill|Sugano no Mamichi|en|Sugano no Mamichi|qid=Q11619464|lt=Sugano no Michimichi}} in the 9th year of the Enryaku era (790 CE), acknowledging his historical mission to Baekje. The {{ill|Sumiyoshi Taisha Shrine Chronicles|ja|住吉大社神代記|1=Sumiyoshi Taisha Shrine Chronicles|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sumiyoshi Taisha Shrine Chronicles|13=User:Immanuelle/Sumiyoshi Taisha Shrine Chronicles|qq=}} also include his name in their accounts of the conquest of Silla.
== Descendant Clans ==
The {{ill|Shinsen Shōjiroku|en|Shinsen Shōjiroku|qid=Q1045362|lt=Shinsen Shōjiroku}} attributes several clans as descendants of Aratawake:
* '''Imperial Lineage:'''
** '''Right Capital Ōno no Ason''': Descended from Toyokiiribiko no Mikoto’s fourth-generation descendant, Ōaratawake no Mikoto.
** '''Right Capital Tanabe no Fuhito''': Descended from Toyokiiribiko no Mikoto’s fourth-generation descendant, Ōaratawake no Mikoto.
** '''Right Capital Sajino no Kimi''': Descended from the same lineage.
** '''Yamato Province Hirokitsuko''': Descended from the same lineage. Related to Toyokiiribiko no Mikoto's fourth-generation descendant, Ōaratawake no Mikoto.
** '''Kawachi Province Tomi no Muraji''': Related to Toyokiiribiko no Mikoto's descendant, Kamitsukeno no Tamichi.
* '''Uncertain Lineage (Miscellaneous Surnames):'''
** '''Kawachi Province Ikei''': Descended from Toyokiiribiko no Mikoto’s fourth-generation descendant, Aratawake no Mikoto.
== Analysis ==
Many clans listed in the {{ill|Shinsen Shōjiroku|en|Shinsen Shōjiroku|qid=Q1045362|lt=Shinsen Shōjiroku}} as descendants of Aratawake were based in Kawachi Province, suggesting that Aratawake is a figure from the traditions of Kawachi’s scribe clans. Some theories link this to the migration of Kawachi clans to the Kamitsukeno region (modern Gunma Prefecture).<ref name="荒田別-氏族"/> 
The historical validity of Empress Jingū’s conquest of Silla is debated, and by extension, the historical existence of Aratawake is uncertain. However, some scholars suggest that early figures involved in diplomacy with Korea are plausible within the Kamitsukeno clan’s narrative.<ref>Mizoguchi Mutsuko, "Aratawake," Asahi Nihon Rekishi Jinmei Jiten.</ref>
The name "Arata" has also been associated with the {{ill|Nitta District, Gunma|en|Nitta District, Gunma|qid=Q7041539|lt=Nitta District}} in {{ill|Kōzuke Province|en|Kōzuke Province|qid=Q1054838|lt=Kōzuke Province}} (present-day {{ill|Ōta, Gunma|en|Ōta, Gunma|qid=Q386179|lt=Ōta, Gunma}}). Some theories propose that Aratawake may have been the interred individual in the massive {{ill|Ōta Tenjinyama Kofun|en|Ōta Tenjinyama Kofun|qid=Q11444167|lt=Ōta Tenjinyama Kofun}}, which dates to the late Kofun period.<ref>Maesawa Terumasa, *Kenokoku no Kenkyū: Kofun Jidai no Kaimei*, Gendai Shichōsha, 1982.</ref>

'''Arata-wake''' (''arata-wake''{{Sfn|荒田別（古代氏族）|2010年}}; {{ill|dates of birth and death unknown|ja|生没年不詳}}) was a {{ill|Kofun period|ja|古墳時代}} {{ill|figure|ja|人物}} appearing in the ''{{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}'' and other texts. Also written '''Arata-wake-no-Mikoto''' or '''Ō-Arata-wake-no-Mikoto'''.

A distant ancestor of the {{ill|Kamitsukenu clan|ja|上毛野氏|lt=Kamitsukenu-no-Kimi|lt_ja=上毛野君}}, he was a {{ill|military commander|ja|武将}} said to have been dispatched to {{ill|Korea|ja|朝鮮}} during the reigns of {{ill|Empress Jingū|ja|神功皇后}} and {{ill|Emperor Ōjin|ja|応神天皇}} (the 15th emperor).

== Records ==
According to the ''{{ill|Nihon Shoki|ja|日本書紀}}'' Empress Jingū Year 49 Month 3 entry, he was appointed general together with {{ill|Shika-wake|ja|鹿我別}} and participated in the campaign against {{ill|Silla|ja|新羅}}. The Empress Jingū Year 50 Month 2 entry records his return.

In the same text's Emperor Ōjin Year 15 Month 8 entry, he was dispatched to {{ill|Baekje|ja|百済}} together with {{ill|Kamu-wake|ja|巫別}}, and in the following year brought back {{ill|Wani|ja|王仁}}. In this entry, Arata-wake and Kamu-wake are described as "ancestors of the Kamitsukenu-no-Kimi."

Moreover, according to the ''{{ill|Shinsen Shōjiroku|ja|新撰姓氏録}}'', he is recorded as the father of {{ill|Kamitsukenu-no-Tamichi|ja|上毛野田道}}. In the ''Nihon Shoki'', Tamichi is described as the younger brother of {{ill|Takehase|ja|竹葉瀬}}, and in the Kenu clan genealogy, Takehase is also transmitted as the son of Arata-wake.

In the ''{{ill|Shoku Nihongi|ja|続日本紀}}'' {{ill|Enryaku|ja|延暦}} 9 ({{ill|790|ja|790年}}) Month 7 entry, the memorial by {{ill|Sugano no Mamichi|ja|菅野真道|lt=Tsu-no-Muraji-Mamichi|lt_ja=津連真道}} and others also mentions Arata-wake's dispatch to Baekje, and the ''{{ill|Sumiyoshi Taisha Jindaiki|ja|住吉大社神代記}}'' also records Arata-wake's name in the legend of the Silla campaign.

== Descendant Clans ==
In the ''{{ill|Shinsen Shōjiroku|ja|新撰姓氏録}}'', the following clans are recorded as descendants.
* Kōbetsu
** Ukyō Ōno-no-Asomi — descendants of Ō-Arata-wake-no-Mikoto, 4th-generation descendant of Toyoki-iri-hiko-no-Mikoto.
** Ukyō Tanabe-no-Fubito — descendants of Ō-Arata-wake-no-Mikoto, 4th-generation descendant of Toyoki-iri-hiko-no-Mikoto.
** Ukyō Sajino-no-Kimi — same as above.
** Yamato Province Hirokitsu-no-Kimi — same ancestor as Shimono-no-Kimi. Descendants of Ō-Arata-wake-no-Mikoto, 4th-generation descendant of Toyoki-iri-hiko-no-Mikoto.
** Kawachi Province Tomi-no-Muraji — same ancestor as Hirokitsu-no-Kimi. Descendants of Toyoki-iri-hiko-no-Mikoto. 4th-generation descendant Arata-wake-no-Mikoto's son {{ill|Tamichi|ja|上毛野田道}}-no-Kimi (omitted below).
* Undetermined Miscellaneous Surnames
** Kawachi Province Ike — descendants of Arata-wake-no-Mikoto, 4th-generation descendant of Toyoki-iri-hiko-no-Mikoto.

== Considerations ==
Since many of the clans recorded in the ''Shinsen Shōjiroku'' are based in Kawachi, there is a theory that Arata-wake was a legendary figure of the Fuhito-lineage clans of Kawachi who claimed descent from {{ill|Wani|ja|王仁}}{{要出典|date=2022年2月}}. Based on this, there is also a theory of clan migration from Kawachi to the {{ill|Kenu|ja|毛野}} region{{Sfn|荒田別（古代氏族）|2010年}}.

Regarding {{ill|Empress Jingū|ja|神功皇后}}'s Silla invasion, there are voices that question the historical validity, and following this, the existence of Arata-wake is also not certain, though some argue it is acceptable to acknowledge that in the early period there were persons among the Kantō powers involved in diplomacy with Korea<ref>Mizoguchi Mutsuko, "Arata-wake" (''Asahi Nihon Rekishi Jinbutsu Jiten'') — [https://kotobank.jp/word/%E8%8D%92%E7%94%B0%E5%88%A5-1051329 entry] on Asahi Shimbun Kotobank.</ref>.

In addition, based on the reading "arata," there is a theory connecting him with {{ill|Nitta District|ja|新田郡}} of {{ill|Kōzuke Province|ja|上野国}} (around present-day {{ill|Ōta, Gunma|ja|太田市|lt=Ōta|lt_ja=太田市}} in {{ill|Gunma Prefecture|ja|群馬県}})<ref>Recorded in ''Nihon Chiri Shiryō'' (from Chapter 3 Section 4, ''Kenu-no-Kuni no Kenkyū: Kofun Jidai no Kaimei'' Part 2).</ref>{{Sfn|荒田別（古代氏族）|2010年}}, and some assert he is the buried person of the {{ill|Ōta Tenjinyama Kofun|ja|太田天神山古墳}}, the largest kofun in eastern Japan, which exists in this area<ref>Maezawa Terumasa, ''Kenu-no-Kuni no Kenkyū: Kofun Jidai no Kaimei'' Part 2 ({{ill|Gendai Shichōsha|ja|現代思潮社}}, 1982), Chapter 3 Section 4, Factors in the Development of Kenu Province.</ref>.
